strengths: The paper addresses a timely and underexplored question: whether the generation-understanding gap in unified MLLMs (e.g., Janus-Pro) can be closed through self-improvement using the model's own understanding branch as an internal reward, without external reward models.

The empirical characterization is informative: the Nonunified score quantifies self-contradiction, and the attribution analysis (weak generation vs. weak understanding, using Qwen2.5-VL-72B as a reference judge) yields a clear and actionable finding that contradiction is mostly due to weak generation.

The theoretical contribution is a reasonable extension of learning-dynamics analysis (Ren & Sutherland) to the multimodal generation/understanding setting, with a linear case study and empirical validation via a top-K proxy metric.

The paper identifies and empirically demonstrates co-degradation under corrupted supervision, and importantly shows that the Nonunified score cannot distinguish co-degradation from co-improvement—a useful cautionary finding for the self-improvement literature.
The curriculum-based online (CLO) strategy is a sensible design motivated directly by the analysis, and shows consistent improvements on both ID and OOD subtasks in Table 3.
weaknesses: Limited evaluation scope: experiments are confined to a single model family (Janus-Pro-1B/7B) and post-training uses only ~700 samples from one subtask (3D Spatial) of T2I-CompBench; generalization of the claims to other unified architectures (Show-o, Chameleon, Emu3) is left entirely to future work, so the significance of the conclusions is constrained.

The 'no external signals' framing is somewhat overstated: the attribution analysis, the WinRate metric for understanding, and the recommended data-quality pre-validation all depend on Qwen2.5-VL-72B as an oracle. Understanding 'improvement' is measured only as agreement with this external judge on self-generated images—a narrow proxy; no standard understanding benchmarks (e.g., MMBench, VQA-style suites) are reported, so it is unclear whether general understanding improves or only judgments on in-distribution generated images.

Generation quality is evaluated almost exclusively via UniDet on T2I-CompBench subtasks; no human evaluation, FID/CLIPScore/ImageReward, or comparisons against strong external-reward baselines beyond a brief T2I-R1 comparison.
Checkpoint selection is done by choosing the epoch with the lowest Nonunified score, which risks test-set selection bias and inflates reported gains.

The empirical support for the learning-dynamics theory is weak: only ~60% of generation-improved samples exhibit the predicted understanding-side dynamics (Table 2), barely above the 50% chance level for binary predictions, and the directly computed ΔG_t shows only 'marginal numerical differences' (Appendix A.2). The theory itself assumes single-token (L=1) sequences, limiting applicability to real image token sequences.

Overlap with concurrent/related self-improvement work (UniRL [17], dual self-rewards [43], HermesFlow [15]) is acknowledged but the differentiation—in particular what is genuinely new relative to UniRL's use of the model's own understanding for post-training—could be sharpened.

Training for 120 epochs on 700 samples with checkpoint cherry-picking raises overfitting concerns, and DPO/SFT gains in Table 3 are modest and sometimes inconsistent (e.g., Nonunified score not always improved by DPO variants; CLO-DPO does not consistently beat DPO).

strengths: Identifies and formalizes an interesting phenomenon (self-contradiction between generation and understanding branches in unified MLLMs) and provides a simple metric (Nonunified score) to quantify it.

The dissection of misalignment causes into 'weak generation' vs. 'weak understanding' using an external judge is a sensible diagnostic, and the finding that most contradictions stem from weak generation is actionable.

Attempts a theoretical account by extending the learning-dynamics framework of Ren & Sutherland to the multimodal setting, and includes the honest observation that unification metrics cannot distinguish co-improvement from co-degradation — a useful cautionary finding.
The co-degradation experiment (corrupted SFT labels on Janus-Pro-1B) is a clean, well-designed sanity experiment that supports the learning-dynamics story.
weaknesses: The central claim of 'self-improvement without any external signals' is undermined throughout: the Qwen2.5-VL-72B external model is used to define the ground truth for the origin analysis, the WinRate oracle, and the recommended safeguard against co-degradation. Without Qwen, the framework cannot even certify that improvement (rather than co-degradation) occurred, so the 'fully self-improvement' framing is overstated.

Evaluation scope is very narrow: experiments are confined to Janus-Pro-1B/7B and essentially one subtask (3D Spatial, 700 samples) of T2I-CompBench; the 'OOD' settings are simply other subtasks of the same benchmark. No standard generation benchmarks (GenEval, DPG-Bench, etc.), no human evaluation, and no other unified architectures (Show-o, Emu3, etc. are deferred to future work).
Checkpoint selection bias: the reported checkpoints are chosen by the lowest Nonunified score, i.e., model selection on the evaluation metric itself, which inflates reported gains.

Novelty is limited: using the model's own understanding branch to label/self-train with SFT/DPO is a straightforward application of existing techniques, and closely related self-improvement work (UniRL, T2I-R1, dual self-rewards [43]) is acknowledged; the curriculum component (CLO) is a standard easy-to-hard schedule applied on top, with modest and mixed gains (e.g., CLO-DPO is worse than DPO on understanding for several subtasks in Table 3).

The theoretical contribution is thin: Proposition 1 is largely a direct transplant of existing learning-dynamics results, relies on a single-token simplification (multi-token deferred to future work, despite images being hundreds/thousands of tokens), and the conclusions drawn are qualitative ('tends to', 'potentially preserving sign consistency') rather than falsifiable predictions; the empirical validation is weak — ~60% agreement in Table 2 and only marginal mean differences in ΔGt in Appendix A.2.

Some supporting evidence is noisy or weakly controlled: WinRate is computed only over changed predictions on the model's own pre-generated images; several Table 3 entries show degradation or inconsistency across metrics; Figure 4 group differences are small and could reflect confounds.

Clarity and polish issues throughout: typos ('imropvement', 'self-improvemnet', 'co-degradations'), caption mismatches (Figure 8 vs. Figure 4 references; Figure 9 cited for results that appear in Figure 5), an oddly labeled/segmented Figure 4 axis, and inconsistent notation (ΔGt/ΔU_t subscripts).

Significance is questionable: given the narrow benchmark scope, the dependence on a much larger external judge, and mixed results, the practical impact of the proposed self-improvement recipe is unclear, and the paper itself characterizes the work as an 'exploratory prelude'.

strengths: The paper identifies and formalizes an interesting and timely phenomenon—self-contradiction between the generation and understanding branches of unified MLLMs—and introduces a simple, interpretable metric (Nonunified score) to quantify it.

The framing of using the stronger branch (understanding) as an internal reward signal to guide the weaker branch (generation), enabling reward-model-free self-improvement, is a clean and practical idea with a clear mechanistic motivation.

The analysis is unusually thorough for this area: the paper decomposes contradiction into weak generation vs. weak understanding, provides a learning-dynamics-based theoretical account (Proposition 1) of co-improvement and co-degradation, and empirically validates the theory with proxy and direct dynamics measurements.

The co-degradation finding is valuable and underexplored: showing that unification metrics alone cannot distinguish co-improvement from co-degradation is a cautionary insight relevant to the broader self-improvement literature.
The curriculum-based online (CLO) strategy is a sensible, well-motivated application of the co-improvement observations, with evaluation on both in-distribution and out-of-distribution tasks.
weaknesses: Evaluation is narrow and potentially circular. Understanding 'improvement' (WinRate) is defined relative to Qwen2.5-VL-72B as the oracle, and the same external model is used to attribute contradiction causes, construct labels, and validate conclusions. No human evaluation or independent oracle is provided, so several central claims hinge on a single external judge that also shapes the training data.

Experimental scope is limited to a single model family (Janus-Pro-1B/7B) trained on only 700 samples from one subtask (3D Spatial) of one benchmark. Generalization across architectures (e.g., Show-o, Emu3, Chameleon), datasets, and prompt types is left to future work, weakening the external validity of the conclusions.

There is a test-set selection concern: checkpoints are selected by lowest Nonunified score, and understanding improvement is measured on the same data distribution used to define the training signal, so apparent co-improvement could partly reflect distribution shift or selection bias rather than genuine capability gains.

The theory is restricted to single-token sequences, one-step dynamics, eNTK/linear approximations, and the understanding distribution is derived via Bayes rule under strong assumptions (uniform prompt prior) that do not reflect how the actual model's understanding branch operates. The gap between the idealized analysis and the empirical system is acknowledged but not bridged.

Absolute gains are modest and inconsistent in places (e.g., CLO-DPO underperforms plain DPO on several OOD tasks and on ID generation), and the improvement mechanism evidence (e.g., ~60% agreement with theoretical predictions, marginal ∆Gt differences in Figure 8) is suggestive rather than conclusive.

The curriculum method is fairly standard (easy-to-hard scheduling) and its novelty relative to existing curriculum post-training work is limited; the contribution there is mostly the data-categorization based on internal branch agreement.

Presentation issues: several typos ('self-imropvement', 'improvemnet', 'Disscusion'), inconsistent figure labeling (Figure 8d caption 'GT = 0' appears inconsistent with the text describing GT = 1), and Figure 9's caption is reused/confused in Appendix A.3.

strengths: Comprehensive and well-motivated empirical study: the paper systematically quantifies the generation-understanding gap across six unified MLLMs and nine subtasks spanning three difficulty levels, and identifies task difficulty as a confounder in measuring non-unification — a careful measurement design that goes beyond prior single-model or single-task observations.

The proposed internal gap-based self-improvement framework is simple, requires no external signals, and delivers strong empirical results (up to +20% generation on T2I-CompBench++), matching or exceeding baselines that rely on multiple external reward models (T2I-R1, Hermesflow).

The discovery and analysis of the co-improvement effect in post-training is a genuinely interesting contribution; the extension of NTK-based learning dynamics theory (Propositions 1-2 under both SFT and DPO, with full derivations in the appendix) provides a principled explanation, supported by targeted empirical evidence (false positive correction accounting for ~80% of understanding gains, similarity proxy analysis).
The curriculum replay mechanism is a natural and well-motivated follow-up from the co-improvement analysis, with supporting evidence that it dynamically expands post-training data (Table 2, Table 9).

Extensive supplementary material: full results across three benchmarks (T2I-CompBench++, GenEval, Science-T2I), human-eval checks of the external judge, ablations on trainable components, curriculum epochs, and external reward comparison, plus complete proofs for SFT and DPO settings.
weaknesses: Metric circularity and judge-dependence concerns: the non-unification score relies on the model's own understanding branch with a single binary scoring prompt, and 'understanding improvement' is measured by agreement with an external judge (Qwen2.5-VL-72B) whose labels are also used for training-time analysis. The very low non-unification scores for Show-o (~0.33%) versus Janus-Pro (~26%) suggest the metric is highly sensitive to the judging prompt/model, weakening the 'widespread non-unification' claim as a general phenomenon.

Potential evaluation contamination: self-improvement is performed on ~6000 T2I-CompBench++ prompts and the main results are reported on T2I-CompBench++ validation; in-domain fine-tuning gains (up to +20%) may partly reflect distributional matching rather than genuine capability gains, making the comparison against external-reward baselines potentially favorable. GenEval and Science-T2I gains are much smaller, consistent with this concern.

Limited model scope: experiments are restricted to two MLLMs (Janus-Pro-7B, Show-o) with very small post-training datasets (226-2265 samples); the authors acknowledge this limitation, but generalization claims (e.g., to BAGEL, EMU3) remain unverified.

Theoretical analysis makes strong assumptions (shared tokenizer, one-step SGD, uniform prompt prior, first-order approximation) and the empirical verification uses prompt/image similarity as a proxy for the eNTK rather than computing it, so the causal link between shared eNTK and co-improvement remains indirect; no direct eNTK measurements are provided.

Some reported results are noisy or hard to interpret: e.g., understanding win rates of 0.00 or 100.00 on specific subtasks (Tables 1, 5-7), occasional understanding drops after self-improvement (e.g., Spatial at 26.67 in Table 5), and DPO-based variants sometimes underperform SFT — these irregularities are not thoroughly discussed.

Several improvements are modest (e.g., overall gains on GenEval and Science-T2I are within a few points), and the correlation statistic (rho = 0.53) is reported without significance testing or sample size details.

strengths: Comprehensive empirical verification of the non-unification phenomenon across six unified MLLMs and nine subtasks of varying difficulty, with a reasonable attempt to control for task difficulty as a confounder.

The internal-gap-based self-improvement framework is simple, well-motivated, and avoids external reward models; gains on T2I-CompBench++ (up to ~20% generation, ~16% unification) are non-trivial and comparable to external-reward baselines such as T2I-R1 and Hermesflow.

The theoretical analysis extending learning-dynamics (eNTK) theory to the multimodal generation-understanding setting, with propositions covering both SFT and DPO, is a nice attempt to explain the co-improvement effect rather than merely reporting it.

Reasonable breadth of supporting experiments: SFT/DPO variants, curriculum replay, ablations on trainable components and curriculum epochs, external-reward comparison, human checks against Qwen-based judgments, and qualitative examples.
The paper is generally clearly written and well-organized, with a logical flow from phenomenon verification to mitigation, explanation, and an improved method.
weaknesses: Limited novelty of the core method: using the model's own understanding branch to score and select generations is essentially rejection sampling / self-rewarding; closely related ideas exist (self-critique in Hermesflow, dual self-rewards in Hong et al. 2025), and the curriculum replay component is a straightforward revisit-and-extend strategy on top of standard SFT.

Evaluation circularity and judge dependence: the entire pipeline (non-unification score, weak generation, win rate, false-positive correction labels) is validated against Qwen2.5-VL-72B, the same external judge that defines ground truth. Win rate excludes ties and depends on the pre-trained model's own generations, making cross-method comparisons hard to interpret.

The claimed co-improvement in understanding is largely restricted to the same prompt-image alignment task used in training (false positive detection on T2I-CompBench-style data); this risks being in-domain overfitting rather than genuine generalization. Standard understanding benchmarks show only marginal gains (typically ~1-3%, sometimes negative on POPE), which does not strongly support the 'understanding also improves' claim.

The theoretical claims are not directly verified: the 'shared eNTK' hypothesis is tested only through proxies (text cosine similarity via MiniLM and image MSE/SSIM), never by actually computing the eNTK. The analysis also relies on strong idealizations (one-step SGD, NTK linearity, uniform prompt prior, shared-tokenizer setting) whose applicability to 7B models trained over 20-30 epochs is questionable.

Self-improvement is validated on only two models (Janus-Pro-7B and Show-o), and Show-o already exhibits near-zero non-unification, so most of its gains are marginal; the authors themselves admit Bagel and other models were left to future work.

DPO results are weak and inconsistent: DPO and C-DPO often underperform SFT, sometimes degrade generation, and several unification scores worsen, which weakens the generality of the framework beyond SFT-based rejection sampling.

Some results are based on very small sample sizes (e.g., Non. scores computed on dozens of samples in GenEval/Science-T2I), producing noisy numbers (0%, 100% win rates) with no variance estimates or statistical significance tests.

The central finding (understanding outperforms generation in unified MLLMs) and the mitigation recipe are heavily foreshadowed by prior work cited by the paper itself; the incremental positioning as 'first systematic quantification' is somewhat thin given the metric is a simple rejection rate.

strengths: The paper is well structured around a clear research question (leveraging the internal generation–understanding gap for self-improvement) and answers it with a complete pipeline: empirical verification, a mitigation method, a mechanistic theory, and a derived curriculum-learning improvement.

The proposed non-unification score is a simple, internal-consistency metric that avoids reliance on external judges for measuring the gap, and the large-scale verification across six unified MLLMs, nine subtasks, and three difficulty levels is a valuable empirical contribution; identifying task difficulty as a confounder and stratifying by difficulty is a thoughtful methodological point.

The core method is simple, training-efficient (7–8 hours on 4 A800s), and does not require external reward models, yet it matches or surpasses external-reward baselines (T2I-R1, Hermesflow) on T2I-CompBench++, GenEval, and Science-T2I, which is a convincing result.

The co-improvement finding is empirically characterized in detail (false positive vs. false negative correction, ~80% gains from false positive correction) and supported by a learning-dynamics analysis extending Ren & Sutherland (2025) to the multimodal setting, with propositions for both SFT and DPO and empirical validation of the eNTK dominance hypothesis; the coupling of theory, proxy measurements, and experiments is unusually thorough.

Comprehensive appendix with full results, hyperparameters, ablations (updated components, curriculum epoch, external-reward comparison), and human checks of the Qwen judge strengthens reproducibility and credibility; the F.3 ablation honestly reports that Qwen-assisted alignment still outperforms self-improvement.
weaknesses: Novelty is moderate: the core idea of using the model's own understanding branch to score and improve generation is closely related to existing work on dual/self-rewards (e.g., Hong et al., 2025) and self-critique pipelines; the paper's differentiation lies mainly in the systematic verification and the theoretical co-improvement analysis rather than the method itself.

There is a tension between the paper's central claim and its evaluation protocol: the paper criticizes prior gap measurements for relying on external estimators, yet the 'Weak Generation' diagnosis, the win-rate metric for understanding gains, and the false-positive/false-negative labels all depend on Qwen2.5-VL-72B as an oracle; the human check shows growing disagreement on hard tasks (19.67%), so key conclusions may inherit Qwen's biases.

The non-unification score is a coarse binary self-judgment that could be gamed (a model could trivially reduce its score by becoming a lenient judge of its own outputs); the paper's safeguards (Qwen agreement, external benchmark gains) partially address this but the metric's standalone validity remains questionable.

The theoretical analysis assumes a shared tokenizer and shared LLM, yet the main experiments are primarily on Janus-Pro, a decoupled architecture; the claimed extension to decoupled designs is asserted (Section 5.2) rather than rigorously established, and idealizations (uniform prompt prior, frozen marginal likelihood terms, one-step SGD, frozen generation head) weaken the direct mapping from theory to the observed co-improvement.

Empirical scope for the improvement experiments is narrow: only two MLLMs (Janus-Pro-7B, Show-o) and small post-training datasets (226–2265 samples); DPO results are weaker and less consistent than SFT (e.g., overall generation gains on GenEval/Science-T2I are marginal), and some understanding subtask win rates fall below 50%, so the generality of the co-improvement claim is not fully established.

Several reported 'unification' gains for Show-o are based on near-zero baseline non-unification scores, making percentage improvements on that model less meaningful; evaluation set sizes for some subtasks (e.g., 49 chemistry prompts) are small enough that differences may not be statistically robust.
Understanding improvements on standard benchmarks are modest (up to ~3% on POPE/MMB/SEED/GQA/MMMU), and the win-rate metric compares only on disagreement cases, which can overstate perceived gains.
